analysis.title: GS Basics Liquidation. 1998 or 2000. VVIX.
key_insights: US equities sold off sharply on 6 Nov 2026: Nasdaq -5.5%, SOX -12%, SPX -4.4%. The day before, AI underperformed while the broader market rallied on a perceived political pivot to the center, led by quality, cyclicals and short covering.

Privorotsky attributes the decline to leveraged ETF rebalancing, with mechanical selling into the close in semis and NDX, combined with negative dealer gamma. He calls this a self-reinforcing liquidation.
VVIX had its largest one-day move since Feb 5, 2018.
The cash franchise net sold $3bn, with Tech (Info Tech + Comm Services) accounting for $2.2bn. The Tech unwind now totals -$27bn since it began, larger than the July technical unwind of -$21bn.
GS AIS says the real problem in semis is the absence of underlying demand, particularly from long-only investors. Multi-strat, quant, long-only and retail are all positioned in the same direction.

The speed and size of the moves point to acute leverage and forced de-grossing. Correlations are rising, momentum is underperforming, the residual leverage factor is selling off and low beta, safety and quality are bid.

He leans toward a 1998-style liquidity event rather than March 2000. In 1998 the Russia default and LTCM were external shocks, US growth stayed intact, and markets recovered once liquidity returned and the Fed eased.
Unlike 2000, today's AI leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets. Delaying data centers does not destroy compute demand, and constrained capacity may improve existing economics.

The uncomfortable parallel with 2000 is the scale of AI spending and the uncertainty around returns. He leans toward a sound growth story being liquidated, but says demand, utilization and returns need to hold.

He lists four concerns behind the AI selloff: insufficient capital to finance the buildout, insufficient revenue to justify it, insufficient power and permitting capacity, and an unsustainable aggregate spending trajectory. He says the market has latched onto power and permitting, arguably the least important.

On politics, he reads Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's comments on data centers as a regulatory reset rather than ideological rejection. He thinks actual spending could surprise positively versus what is now discounted.

Oil rebounded roughly 4% the previous day and is higher again. He says markets got ahead of themselves in pricing an immediate Iran off-ramp, negotiations remain unresolved, and the energy shock complicates stabilization in rates, growth expectations and risk appetite.
Nasdaq has broken its 200-day moving average and the S&P sits just above it, which he says needs to hold. Negative gamma leaves room for violent moves in either direction.

He thinks the last leg down has overextended in a number of assets as forced de-risking entrenched, and points to higher-quality tech such as TSMC and ASML. He expects participants to play defense into the weekend, but says such episodes have historically been buying opportunities.

He says the narrative would change on political reflexivity around AI investment, stabilization in funding markets, and evidence that spending and demand remain intact. He stands by his pre-election view and cites the S&P being higher 12 months after all 19 midterms since 1950, which he calls a 12-month observation and not a one-month forecast.

tension_points.bull_case: Like 1998, the shock is external and financing-driven while the growth engine stays intact. Today's AI leaders have real revenues, cash flows and balance sheets, and delayed data centers do not destroy compute demand. Privorotsky leans this way.
tension_points.bear_case: Like March 2000, this could be the start of a structural technology unwind. The scale of spending and the uncertainty around returns are the uncomfortable parallel.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Demand, utilization and returns failing to hold. He also says the S&P needs to hold just above its 200-day moving average.

tension_points.bull_case: Constrained supply is not disappearing demand, and capacity limits may improve existing economics. Texas rhetoric reads as a regulatory reset, so actual spending could surprise positively.
tension_points.bear_case: If data center construction slows dramatically, nominal growth expectations look unrealistic and the cyclicals that rallied look mispriced. GS AIS flags an absence of underlying demand in semis.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that underlying spending and demand are not intact, or no stabilization in funding markets.

theme_stances.key_argument: The AI growth engine may stay intact even as markets reprice the financing and timing of the buildout.
The governor-elect's rhetoric points to a regulatory reset, so spending could surprise positively versus what is discounted.
theme_stances.evidence: It is not that I hate data centers.
